alt: Overlapping circles: deviance breaks norms, crime breaks the law, and most crime falls in the overlap. Talking loudly in a library is deviant but not criminal; minor speeding is criminal but barely deviant. Below, relativity between societies, within a society, by situation and across time.
caption: Most crime is deviant, but not all deviance is crime, and both depend on context.

alt: Durkheim argued some crime is normal and functional, reminding people of shared rules and prompting change. Becker argued deviance is a label applied by others, with powerful groups deciding which acts are labelled.
caption: Durkheim explains why crime exists; Becker explains who defines it.

alt: Formal control by the police, courts, armed forces, government and penal system, each with its method; informal control by family, education, workplace, peer group, media and religion through sanctions such as praise, ridicule, dismissal and public shaming.
caption: Formal control comes from the state; informal control comes from everyday relationships.

alt: Hirschi’s four bonds (attachment, commitment, involvement, belief) explain why most people conform. A balance weighs informal control (constant and internalised) against formal control (needed for those not reached and for serious crime, plus surveillance), with limits of both.
caption: Strong bonds do most of the work; formal control catches what they miss.

alt: Eleven crime types with an example each: violent, property, white-collar or corporate, expressive, instrumental, gang, green, global or organised, cyber, hate and domestic. A worked stimulus shows one incident fitting several types: a theft that is property and instrumental crime, and online posts that may be hate and cyber crime.
caption: One incident can fit several crime types at once.

alt: Nested bars narrow from all crime, to crime experienced by victims who know, to crime reported, to crime recorded by police. Self-report studies reach offending at the widest level, victim surveys reach crime victims know about, and official statistics show only recorded crime. Reasons for unreported and unrecorded crime are listed below.
caption: Each measure sees a different slice; none sees the dark figure fully.

alt: Official statistics, self-report studies and victim surveys compared on strengths and limitations, with national and local victim survey examples: the Crime Survey for England and Wales and the Islington Crime Survey.
caption: Compare at least two methods when discussing measurement.
